result:
The night the power went out, our street emptied onto its own lawns. It was summer, nearly midnight, and the darkness had a texture to it—thick, warm, unfamiliar. Nobody had seen the stars from their own front yard in years.

Mr. Halloran brought out a battery radio and found a station playing old doo-wop. The Delgado kids, who I'd only ever seen as silhouettes behind school bus windows, were catching fireflies in a jar, their laughter carrying the way sound does when there's no refrigerator hum to swallow it.

Someone said the grid had failed three counties over. Someone else blamed a solar flare. It didn't matter. What mattered was that Mrs. Okafor, who had lived at the end of the block for eleven years without our ever learning her first name, turned out to be funny—dry and quick, with stories about Lagos in the seventies that made her sound like a different person entirely, or maybe the same person, finally legible.

The power came back around two in the morning. I remember the exact moment: every window on the street flickering to life at once, blue and electric, like the houses had opened their eyes. We all stood there a second, blinking, slightly blinded. Then, one by one, we drifted back inside, back into our separate brightnesses.

Nobody ever organized the block party we'd half-promised each other. But for weeks afterward, people waved. They asked about each other's gardens, each other's kids. Small things. But in the dark, we had learned each other's names, and that counted for something.
